utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. You're continuing with your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Simeunovic.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Before we adjourned on Wednesday, you spoke about the arrival and reception of detainees in the Brcko garrison. Can you please continue with that subject? What was the reception like? What did you see there? What did you do? What steps did you take to ensure that everything went smoothly?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already explained that I was very surprised by our arrival in Brcko and by the way the military police received the detainees. The commander of the military police from the Brcko garrison his name was Tegeltija. I spoke to the commander and I insisted that they change the way they started treating the people I had brought along from Samac. I pleaded with him for a more humane treatment, for people to simply be received and accommodated in their premises. He tried to explain: "Well, Makso, you know what the procedure is like. We must search these people." And I told him: "If you must search these people, search them, but they're coming from detention. That's one thing you must bear in mind. However, do whatever you see fit and follow your usual procedure." However, as we talked about this, I remember one policeman hit one of the men who had already been searched, in the head, and the man banged against a wall. His nose started bleeding. My reaction was to tell Tegeltija -- I stepped back from him as I was carrying a Heckler, an automatic weapon. I pointed my Heckler at him and I said: "Tegeltija, you should cut this out right now, what you're doing to these people." He tried to calm me down. He said: "Take it easy, Makso. Take it easy, Maksim. You aren't going to use that gun, are you?" But the only thing I wanted him to do is to treat the detainees who I brought along in a more humane way. So the treatment changed after my request. People were still being searched, but they -- their hands were no longer being tied behind their backs. They would merely search them and take them to the room that had been prepared for that purpose. Once this reception was over, I went looking for Captain Petrovic at the garrison command in Brcko. I found him and I told him the whole story. I told him about my reaction. I told Captain Petrovic to make sure those people received food and water. This was already in the evening. I told him to make sure they got food and water. And he said: "Okay. Simo Zaric already called me, asking if you have already arrived." And he asked me the same thing, for food and water to be given these people. And he also asked for medical assistance for these people, as all those people had been beaten black and blue when they came from Samac. He knew, because he had seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This space inside which they were accommodated, what sort of building was that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were rooms that were actually used as warehouses, storages for the companies. The companies would leave their equipment and ammunition in those rooms. At that point, the rooms were empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you see on the windows of that building?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were bars on the windows. That was the storage rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain what sort of bars they were.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bars on the warehouse windows, they were not put there once they found out about the detainees coming in. The bars had been there before, when the rooms were still being used as warehouses. They were on the inside of the window, not on the outside, to make sure no one was able to remove the bars and enter the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Captain Petrovic complied with everything that he had promised? Were people given food, water, and medical assistance eventually?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day I found out that they had received food and water and that a doctor had arrived from the garrison medical station, that he gave the detainees a medical check and that he had treated some of their wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you report to Commander Nikolic about the completion of this task?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After my conversation with Captain Petrovic, at the garrison command in Brcko, I returned to the command post of the 17th Tactical Group in Pelagicevo and I reported to Commander Nikolic, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic. I told him that my task had been completed and that all the people had been transferred. I told him there hadn't been any trouble, and what I meant was that we had not had any trouble with the volunteers in Samac. I also told him briefly about the reception in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After the detainees had been accommodated in the Brcko garrison, did you have any further contact with those detainees?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no further contact with them, because now they were under the authority of the security organs of the 395th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that they were no longer within the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were no longer within the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group. Now they were in the area of responsibility of the 395th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened later to those people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Before you go on to that point: For those of us who are not that familiar with the motorised brigades of the JNA and so on, perhaps the witness could just elaborate very briefly. The 395th Motorised Brigade, the commander of which, who was he or she responsible to? Just so that we have a sense what this motorised brigade was responsible to and, you know, where it fits in the bigger scheme of things that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, you have heard the question by the Honourable Judge Williams. You have heard what she wants to know. Can you please tell us about the motorised Brigade? Where was its area of responsibility? Where was its headquarters? Who was the commander, and which was their Superior Command at the time?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command headquarters of the 395th Motorised Brigade was in the town of Brcko. Its area of responsibility was to the east of the border of the Brcko municipality, that's the right-hand boundary of Bijeljina municipality, the village of Bukovice, more specifically. The border to the west -- to the west, they bordered with the 317th Tactical Group [As interpreted]. That is the village lying between the village of Gorice and the village of Krepsici. Along the depth, the border was the village of Pukis, which was about 13 kilometres from Brcko, and in front there was the River Sava, the boundary with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just one correction for the transcript. On page 5, line 13, it's 17th Tactical Group, not 317th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. It will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And also in response to my question, I asked: Who did they report to? Who was sort of superior to the head of this 395th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. The question has already been posed, but I may have misheard, but I think not. I think the witness said to the west there was the village of Bukovice.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The to the east the village of Bukovice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please continue now? Who was the commander, and who were they subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 395th Motorised Brigade was Lieutenant Colonel Pavle Milinkovic. The Superior Command was the 17th Corps, based in Tuzla, with headquarters in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the command of the 395th Motorised Brigade reported to the command of the 17th Corps in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. That was their Superior Command, the Superior Command of the 395th Motorised Brigade, the command of the 17th Corps based in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And who was the person in charge of the 17th Corps in Tuzla, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The corps commander, that was General Sava Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The next question I want to ask -- in fact, I've already asked you: Do you know what later happened to those detainees?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, when hostilities broke out in the town of Brcko, on the 1st of May, 1992, the detainees who had arrived from Samac, for safety reasons, for security reasons, they were transferred to the Bijeljina garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We'll switch now to an event which took place in Crkvina, which is a village in Samac municipality. When murders were committed, do you know anything about that event, and how did you find out about it?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. I know what happened in the village of Crkvina, Bosanski Samac municipality. The person who informed me about that was the assistant commander for intelligence and security in the 4th Detachment of the JNA, Simo Zaric. That occurred on the 8th -- actually, on the morning of the 9th. Simo Zaric phoned me at the command and he told me: Look, Makso - perhaps not in as many words, but he said. A crime had been committed in Crkvina, that people had been killed. He told me that and he kept on speaking, and I tried to tell him: "Take it easy, Simo. Here, the commander is here. He's awake. So I think you should tell him what you just told me." I didn't ask any further questions. I just put him through to the commander directly so that he could talk to Simo Zaric about what happened. That means I already knew that a crime had taken place, because Simo had told me. Then he went on to speak to the commander, and I noticed that the commander was trying to soothe him, to calm him down, because Simo sounded quite agitated. You couldn't interrupt him. He spoke on and on. He was probably saying that there were lives to be saved and that the whole thing was to be prevented, that people had to be protected, and asked how long this was going to last. I was judging on the basis of the answers that the commander was giving him. He said: "Take it easy, Simo. We'll just look into what happened and then we'll do something to keep this sort of thing from recurring." And then he told him to come to the command of the 17th Tactical Group, and the next morning, Simo arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Commander Nikolic and Simo Zaric talk about then, and were you there during their conversation?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there in the office at the command, alongside with some other members of the 17th Tactical Group. The commander and Simo Zaric talked about the incident. Simo Zaric filled him in again on the details of the incident. He told him how he had found out about it and what exactly had happened. He was not quite calm yet. He was still rather agitated. But he was able to provide more detail on what had happened and how he had found out about it. He told the commander that, on his way back from a mission, he reached the checkpoint in Crkvina - the checkpoint was still there - and he was stopped by a police officer, who told him that Lugar, the forest keeper, was at a centre there where people were being kept in detention. He told him that he had killed 16 people, Lugar. And Simo then told him that he couldn't believe it, and whether he knew who had done that. And then he told him that the murders had been committed by a volunteer who arrived there, and that the name of that volunteer was Lugar. Simo asked him if anyone else knew about this, and then he told him that he didn't know whether anyone else knew about this, about the crime. He was probably referring to the authorities in Samac or to the command of the 17th Tactical Group, or perhaps the 4th Detachment. Then he told him: Blagoje Simic just passed by on his way to another detachment. Simo Zaric set out because the detachment was not far from there and he said that he found Blagoje Simic at the command of the detachment and that he told him about what had occurred. Blagoje seemed surprised by what he heard from Simo, and he said: "Well, what are they doing to us? How long is this going to last?" Something along those lines. After that, I mean, that is what Simo told the commander, he asked the commander to go to Belgrade. He asked for permission - let's put it that way - and he said: "Commander, I would like to go to Belgrade. I would like to convey to the highest authorities in the army of Yugoslavia, the highest security organs in the army of Yugoslavia, what happened, what crime was committed, and I want to seek protection."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's just a matter of accuracy of transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When the witness was referring to that detachment in Crkvina, he said "Drugi Odred" meaning 2nd Detachment, not another detachment, because this was a village where actually 2nd Detachment was placed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please proceed. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo asked the commander for permission so that he could go to Belgrade to provide this information. He said: "I know Colonel Jugoslav Maksimovic, who works at the General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army at Belgrade. He works on security matters. I'm going to go and see him and convey to him what has been going on." Jugoslav was from the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, so he knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Zaric go to Belgrade? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zaric went, given the permission of the commander. He went to Belgrade to talk about what had happened in Crkvina. I did not mention one thing, though, that after Simo Zaric called, Commander Nikolic immediately informed his Superior Command about this crime. I omitted to mention that in the sequence of my recount. So Simo was given permission by the commander, and indeed he went on the 9th to Belgrade, to the General Staff, to the security department of the General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army. He went to find this Colonel Jugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When Zaric returned from Belgrade, did he report to you and to the commander about what he had done in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after returning from Belgrade, Simo stopped at the command. He first came to the command of the 17th Tactical Group, and he said to the commander what he had done and what he had conveyed to the people there, that is to say, the generals of the General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army. He said that he first went to see Colonel Jugoslav Maksimovic because he knew him personally. He told him about this event, and Colonel Jugoslav took him to General Vasiljevic, who was deputy head of security in the General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army. They conveyed to him as well what had happened in Crkvina. Whether he had heard about it or something. But anyway, General Vasiljevic came too, head of security of the General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army. He also came to this office. And they acquainted him with this case as well. Simo said to the commander that an official note had been compiled about that, about what he had conveyed to them there in that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. You mentioned two generals, and you said that Vasiljevic was both of their last names. Were both generals Vasiljevic or was one of them only Vasiljevic, and what was the last name of the other general?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Jugoslav took him to General Gligorevic, Gligorevic, who was assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now: Did you, that is, the security organ of the 17th Tactical Brigade, did you carry out any investigation in relation to the crime in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not carry out any investigation with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me why you didn't carry out any investigation?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not carry out an investigation because when Commander Nikolic informed his Superior Command, and when he said to them that a crime had been committed by a member of the volunteers, who was not a member of the Yugoslav People's Army, who is under the police in Samac, it was said that we could not carry out any investigation if the crime was not committed by a member of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about an event when members of these volunteers physically abused the commander of the 4th Detachment, Radovan Antic, Captain Radovan Antic?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that too. I mean, I'm aware of that event. I know about what happened and how it happened. This was conveyed to me by Simo Zaric as well and I heard about it from other people too who were there, that Lugar and some other specials walked into the command of the 4th Detachment, that they simply lined up the command - how should I put this? - that they knocked out the commander of the 4th Detachment, Radovan Antic. After that, they took him to Obudovac, the village of Obudovac, and he was detained there in an outhouse, and he was kept there, locked up, for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just interested in whether you knew something about that. Can we please go back now to some matters that we've already gone through. I would like to show a document to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Before we move on: On page 12, line 3, is it they locked out the commander, they knocked him out physically, punching him and he became unconscious? They locked him out of the headquarters? Could we have some clarification on this, please? It's not clear happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You were not present there. You are just conveying what you were told. Do you know whether Commander Antic was unconscious? Where was he locked up? And then, when was he released from the place where he had been locked up?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present when this actually happened. I am talking about what I heard from others. He was hit, punched, knocked out. And now, whether he was unconscious at that moment or not, I don't know, but I do know that after that knockout, after he was hit in the face with a fist, he was taken to the village of Obudovac and then he was locked up in an outhouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How long was he detained in that outhouse?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while, about two or three hours, to the best of my knowledge. That's what I found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we're talking about the involvement of the Party of Democratic Action in training and armament, I would actually in this connection like to introduce a document. This is document PDB 1/3 ter. I think that all parties in the proceedings have this document. So could a copy please be placed before the witness so that we could discuss it a bit. Mr. Simeunovic, please take a look at this document. Please look at its contents and then we'll discuss it. Tell us, please: What does it say in the upper left-hand corner of this document?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner it says: The SDA, Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. And what does it say underneath, addressed to, et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Addressed to -- this is probably the addressee -- the Executive Board of the SDA, that is to say, the Party of Democratic Action, to the president, personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the subject here.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says here: "Instructions for sending candidates to the training centre of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: There is a date on the right-hand side. Could you please read the date.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 11th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What's the stamp down here? What does it say on the stamp, if you can read it?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the middle it says "the SDA Sarajevo," and around it it says: "Party of Democratic Action."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And in the right-hand corner there is a signature?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "On behalf of, acting secretary of the SDA, Hasan Cengic," and then there is the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You have familiarised yourself with the contents of this document; right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion during your work to find other such documents or similar documents? And please tell us: What is sought through this document, and who is sending candidates for training to the training centre of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke on Wednesday about armament -- illegal armament and about sending people for training -- these people later returned as -- I mean, these were candidates who were trained for commanding lower-ranking units. Then I said that it was political parties who were sending these people. We see here in this document that it says that it is the duty of every candidate to take along the referral of the political party that is sending him, that is making this proposal for him to be sent for training at the training centre of the MUP of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Does this pertain to candidates that are sent by the Party of Democratic Action? They have to be members of the party of democratic action?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this case, it is requested that the candidate who is being sent is sent by the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We won't be needing the document any longer. I would just like to be asked for a number to be given to it. I would like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D41/4, and ter for the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, do you know about the activities surrounding the withdrawal of the JNA from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the activities surrounding the withdrawal of the JNA from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Even before the official order came in, we had already heard about the JNA being withdrawn from Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was towards the end of April, and we did have some information on that, but no accurate information. We did know that it would happen, but we did not know at that point when exactly it would happen. At the beginning of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, ask your client to deal with facts what happened. He should just narrow it to what happened instead of going into these details they didn't know what would happen and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. Just correction to the transcript. Not his client, his witness, just to be precise, maybe, to avoid misunderstanding. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You needn't go into any details. Just tell us what you know about the withdrawal, how it went. Were there any problems when manpower was being evacuated, and equipment too? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an order from the General Staff of the JNA. It arrived at the beginning of May 1992. Pursuant to this order, all commissioned officers who were not from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who were not born in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were to withdraw by the 19th of May, 1992, and that they were to report to the 31st Personnel Centre in Belgrade. To report to the 31st Personnel Centre would have meant that they had left the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did soldiers of the JNA have the same obligation?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This applied to soldiers too. However, in our area of responsibility, there were no soldiers; there were only commissioned officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about any activities undertaken to prevent the JNA leaving the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina with its manpower and all its equipment?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We learned that an order had been issued for all roads to be blocked when the JNA started leaving. This was an attempt to prevent the weapons and equipment they had from being taken out of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Exits from the barracks were to be blocked too. This applied to the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you know of any specific action being taken in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When, on the 15th of May, a convoy of soldiers and commissioned officers of the JNA tried to leave the Tuzla garrison, and following the orders received from the General Staff, tried to return to Serbia, to the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the convoy was attacked by the SDA, by the Party of Democratic Action, and other paramilitary units in Tuzla. On that occasion --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would move to strike his statement: "Attacked by SDA or paramilitary units." At this point you have a legitimate government of Bosnia-Herzegovina that has been recognised by the United States, by the European Union, and because they're not JNA units, it doesn't make them paramilitary units. So I'd move to strike that. And admitted to the United Nations too at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is our point of view that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina recognised and accepted by the United Nations on the 11th of May, 1992, only became a sovereign state at that point in time, and it was only then that it could have its own army and other bodies. This is a fact. No, the 22nd. Bosnia and Herzegovina became a member of the United Nations on the 22nd of May, 1992, and all the actions taken against the JNA and civilian persons, we believe that individuals and organisations who were not constitutional were to blame for all those actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. I just want to make sure I understand you correctly. Are you saying, as a matter of public international law, based on state practice and opinio juris, that it is only when an entity becomes a member of the United Nations that it is a sovereign state? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position is that if a sovereign state falls apart, such as the Socialist Federal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. I'm not asking you that. I'm not asking about disintegration of states. I'm going back to exactly the point that you made on page 17, your answer, lines 21 to 25. You're saying that -- excuse me. I have a bit of a cold, so I apologise for my voice here. You're saying that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina only became a sovereign state at the point in time when it was recognised and accepted by the United Nations. And then there was some confusion on the dates, but then you point to the 22nd of May. So I'm asking you: Are you saying statehood is predicated on acceptance to the United Nations -- by the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council? Is that your position? A simple question. I'd just like to know for the sake of clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put it this way: In addition to all the other conditions indicating the existence of international statehood, I think admission into the United Nations is also one such condition whereby a state fully completes its international sovereignty and international statehood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: But on the other hand, Mr. Pisarevic, if an entity, for maybe political reasons, is not voted in by the Security Council and the General Assembly but is de facto in control of territory with a population, a government willing and able to enter into relations with other countries, and is also recognised by neighbouring states and other parts of the world community, even without United Nations membership, presumably it's in existence. So I leave that with you for maybe your arguments later on, but I don't think, to be quite clear, that acceptance and membership in the United Nations is the be all and the end all. For example, we've had Switzerland. Switzerland has only just become a member of the United Nations, but nobody would ever decry the issue that Switzerland is a sovereign state. Anyway, I'll let you get on with your arguments, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. It is not my intention to dispute what you've just said, but I think this is an issue for a wider discussion, and we are dealing with a specific situation here with this witness. However, these issues may come up again during our defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us briefly what happened, disregarding for the moment whether those were paramilitary forces or other kinds of forces? What did you know about this incident when the JNA was attacked during its withdrawal from Bosnia-Herzegovina and as it was complying with its duty to return to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about a convoy being attacked in Tuzla as it was leaving the JNA barracks in Tuzla. The convoy was attacked by -- I'm just using the term "paramilitary units" because those units were not under the command of the JNA. As I myself was an officer, for me, they were paramilitary units. The civilian police of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was taking part in this too, preventing soldiers from exiting the barracks. On that occasion, many soldiers were killed. I know that 56 soldiers were missing from the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show the witness document PDB 6/3 ter. Can the witness please be shown this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Will you please take a minute to familiarise yourself with this document. Can we proceed now please?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it says in the upper left-hand corner of the document?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner, it reads: "MUP of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." The number is 10-70 and the date is 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read who the addressees are of this document.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The addressees are CSB, Security Services Centre, to all, and to the chief, public security stations, to all and to the chief; and to the Sarajevo SUP, the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After the first passage, the first word of the following one is order.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Order on the implementation of the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, number 02-11-327/92."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what you can read in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the middle of the page it reads: "I hereby order ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What follows from this order? What exactly is being ordered here?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under number 1, we can read: "Carry out complete and massive blocking on all roads in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina being used by units of the former JNA to evacuate their technical and materiel equipment. Carry out this order in direct coordination with the Ministry of the Interior."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what it says in the lower right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Minister of Internal Affairs, Alija Delimustafic."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this order was applied against members of the JNA on their way out?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that it was carried out. I know about what happened in Tuzla. I know about another incident in Dobrovoljacka Street in Sarajevo, where there were a lot of casualties among the JNA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: But locally?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even in Brcko itself, there were a number of incidents where rallies were organised outside the JNA barracks. The parties organised them. They said that their sons and brothers were being sent to the front lines in the Republic of Croatia. Those were mass rallies. And I remember when it was approved that whoever had a brother, son, or grandson could enter the JNA barracks, displaying his ID on the way in and to check where their respective son or grandson or brother was. So only two or three people among the 800 or thousand who were standing outside the barracks actually came in to check. Everyone else had merely been manipulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the warehouse being attacked, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the warehouse in Krepsic was attacked. This warehouse was in the area of responsibility of the 395th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll no longer be needing this document. I'd just like to have a number given to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection to this document, which indicates that it's from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, it should be, for clarification, there should be some clarification made as part of this document that this occurs two days after the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is proclaimed on 27 April 1992. So it should be placed in context, that these things are happening right after the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is proclaimed, which is Serbia and Montenegro, and a new constitution has been adopted. There's much more context to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D42/4 and D42/4 ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us now, please, specifically: When did the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA leave Pelagicevo? When did it cease to exist?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those officers who were not originally from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and who were members of the 17th Tactical Group left on the 19th of May, 1992. They went to the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Among those officers, was the commander of the 17th Tactical Group Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic also among them?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander, Commander Stevan Nikolic, was among the officers who left. Major Brajkovic was among them too. And all the officers who originally hailed from Serbia, or any of the other republics, all those who were not originally from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, left the 17th Tactical Group following the orders they had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, on that day when they left, the 17th Tactical Group of the Yugoslav People's Army ceased to exist. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be put that way, that it then ceased. As for the command of the Tactical Group, the 17th Tactical Group, the chief of artillery remained, and I did, as head of the security and intelligence organ. There weren't any other officers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that the witness mentioned the name of the chief of artillery, and I don't see this in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic can ask the witness whether that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the head of the 17th Tactical Group? Major --?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the 17th Tactical Group was Captain Sabrija.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was head --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Was this the chief of artillery? Because that was what Mr. Pisarevic was talking about. And the witness had said the chief of artillery remained. So is this the correct name?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the chief of artillery of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the artillery of the 17th Tactical Group was Sabrija, and he remained after this group of officers left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of Chief Sabrija?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an ethnic Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You said that you remained as chief for intelligence and security affairs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it was only Sabrija, chief of artillery, and I, as chief for security and intelligence affairs, we were the only officers who remained in the command of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Why was it that only you and Sabrija remained?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We remained because we had been born in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a few more questions in this regard. There was this armoured battalion. People who were in this armoured battalion, the tank crews, et cetera, where did these people come from?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crews in the armoured battalion were from the area of the municipalities of Brcko, Samac, Gradacac, Orasje, those municipalities. Except for some officers who had been born in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: These officers of the Yugoslav People's Army who had been born in Serbia, did they have any possibility to transport this equipment, this armour, to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they had no such possibility. I've already said that in the 17th Tactical Group, there had been no conscripts. There were only officers and non-commissioned officers there. There weren't there many of them either. They were not in a position to take anything, because a tank could only be driven by a tank driver. It was impossible for them to drive away this kind of equipment, technical equipment, and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, where was that established, of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Infantry Brigade was established instead of the former 17th Tactical Group of the former Yugoslav People's Army, so it was the 2nd Posavina Brigade of the army of Republika Srpska that was established. It was established after the 19th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When was the new command established in this 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade of the army of Republika Srpska? How did that take place?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the officers who had not been born in Bosnia and Herzegovina left, I already said that it was the chief of artillery and I that stayed behind at the command as officers. Immediately after that, perhaps the following day or two days later, Major Jovica Savic came to the command post in the village of Pelagicevo. He said that he had orders from the command, at that time, the East Bosnian Corps had been established already instead of the 17th Corps. The 17th Corps went to the territory of the municipality of Ugljevik. Well, that he had orders stating that he was appointed commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. After some 30 or 40 minutes, just after he had settled in and after I showed him where he would be staying, Major Jovica Savic came to the command post -- then it was that Srecko Radovanovic, Debeli, came to the command post. That's what happened then. And he said that he also had orders appointing him commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. So at one moment, I had - let's put it this way - two commanders, two brigade commanders. When Srecko Radovanovic came to the command post, Major Jovica was standing in front of the command building. He passed by the major and then he turned around, looked at him - he knew me; he did not know him - and he asked: "What are you doing here?" Major Savic answered: "I have been appointed commander of the brigade." Then the other one gave a vulgar response. He cursed him and said: "What do you mean? What kind of a commander are you? I was appointed commander." Srecko Radovanovic stayed at the command post for a very short while and then he left. He said goodbye to me because he knew me, because we had met before. Major Jovica Savic stayed for a while. Nobody even knew him at the command. And quite simply, he just asked: "Where could I make a phone call from? I should like to phone my command." I took him to the office and he phoned some superior officer at the command. I don't know who exactly. I was not present while the conversation took place. I just brought him into the room and then I went out. After the conversation took place, Major Jovica Savic said to me: "I will no longer be commander. That is what the superior officer said. A vehicle is going to come and fetch me and then I'm going." After perhaps an hour and a half, a vehicle came and he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you see these orders pertaining to these appointments? Did they take some piece of paper out and show it to you when they were introducing themselves?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did take out a sheet of paper, but I didn't look at it, and I did not see who appointed Major Jovica Savic, whose stamp was there, and on whose orders he was appointed. I also did not look at the orders of Srecko Radovanovic. They just said that they had this, and it was not my duty to check on the orders appointing commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So did Srecko Radovanovic really come as commander, after Major Jovica Savic left?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Srecko Radovanovic did not come, and he did not become commander. He did not become commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who came as commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade after all of this happened?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this case, if I can put it that way, when I had two commanders in one day, Mico -- just a moment, please. I know the man. I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was it perhaps Colonel Mico Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Colonel Mico Djurdjevic came with orders appointing him commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. Afterwards I found out that Mico Djurdjevic was from the area, that he was born in the village of Tisina, in the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What were the first actions taken by the new commander, Colonel Mico Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Colonel Djurdjevic came to the command post - I was head of the security and intelligence department, and he invited me, and I briefly presented to him the intelligence situation, but primarily the security situation in this area of responsibility. While I was making this presentation, I saw that he was very familiar with everything that had been taking place within the zone of responsibility, the area of responsibility. He immediately embarked upon the establishment of the brigade, that is to say, the remaining officer personnel in the 2nd Posavina Brigade. He also immediately asked for a meeting to be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: At the command of the brigade, did you continue to be head of security and intelligence affairs?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After Mico Djurdjevic came, I remained head of security and intelligence, but Sabrija also stayed on as head of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And was a meeting organised, and with whom? Did the commander organise a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander, soon after his arrival at the command post, a day or two later, he held a meeting at the premises of the local office in Pelagicevo. It was like the premises of the local community where the local people used to gather. Everybody was invited to that meeting, that is to say, all the commanders of the detachments. Detachments were now re-established as battalions. All assistants for intelligence and security affairs were invited. Also the civilian authorities were invited of the Serb municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo, under formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was present at that meeting on behalf of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On behalf of the civilian authorities of the Serb municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation, I know that the following persons were present: Blagoje Simic, Stevan Todorovic. I think that Milan Blagojevic was present too, some other people from Samac were present, who I did not know. From Pelagicevo there was Dusan Tanasic. He was there. I did not know many people from Samac, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did the commander say at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting, the commander familiarised all persons present with the order pertaining to his appointment as commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. He briefly presented what he knew about the security situation. He particularly referred to the group of volunteers who had come in the month of April and who were in Samac. He asked that these volunteers be placed under the command of the army of Republika Srpska, that they be placed under his command. Or, if they did not wish to be placed under the command of the army of Republika Srpska, that they should leave, that they would have to leave the territory of that area of responsibility, or that they strictly be placed under the control of the civilian police and that they should wear their uniforms too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that meeting, did the commander receive support from all persons present?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what he asked for, that everybody state their views as to whether they were in favour of what he had said, the way he had put it, the way he wanted things to evolve and the future. He wanted to have the situation under his control within his area of responsibility. He said that he would prevent lootings that did take place, and he asked for support and he received that support from the persons who were present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you know what happened after the fall?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the meeting that was held in Pelagicevo, life somehow changed in all the units of the army of Republika Srpska and in the territory involved. However, after six or seven days, after Commander Djurdjevic came to command the 2nd Posavina Brigade, he said to me: "I have been invited to the Crisis Staff, to the premises of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Samac, to go to a meeting there." And then: "Could you please come with me."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time for our break now, so we'll continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may: Page 30, line 14: Instead of word "fall" at the end of the sentence, it should be: After a couple of days. Because that's exactly what my learned friend asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. That will be corrected. We'll take our break and continue at 1615.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, you spoke about Djurdjevic asking whether you could come with him. Can you please tell us what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander was on his way, and he asked me to come along to the meeting at the Crisis Staff building, the Crisis Staff of Samac municipality. In the same vehicle, we were accompanied by two military police officers. They were escorting the commander. We set out, and I asked the commander, and he told me that he had no idea what the meeting would be about, but he invited me to come along. We reached the Crisis Staff premises in Samac. That's where the Crisis Staff building was in Samac. I noticed a large group of people wearing camouflage uniforms. Those were volunteers who had arrived on the 11th of April. There were some other people there who were still being trained. They had arrived with them, but they were from the area of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just one small intervention in the transcript. The premises that were mentioned by the witness were heating plants in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After arriving at the Crisis Staff premises, at the heating plant in Samac, we left our vehicle, and together with Commander Djurdjevic, I tried to go into the building, to enter the heating plant building. The security who were there, they were probably providing security for the Crisis Staff, would not allow me into the building. They said that only the commander could go to the meeting, and you, they told me, will stay outside and wait. I protested. I thought there was no reason for me to stay outside. And Djurdjevic, in order to calm the situation down, told me to just wait outside near the vehicle, and that's what I did. I returned to where we had left our vehicle. It was the month of May, sunny weather, but the driver had moved the vehicle into the shade. We were not parked directly outside the building. It was a little bit to the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How long did you wait for Commander Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reckon it must have been between one and a half and two hours. That's my estimate. During that time, the military policeman -- one of the military police officers would come out to see whether maybe the meeting was finished, and I was waiting by the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When the commander -- when did the commander turn up?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After about one and a half or two hours, the commander came out, and the driver headed towards him immediately. I didn't enter the vehicle. I was still standing outside. And I saw that the commander was agitated. I could tell by the way he acted that something had happened. By looking at his face, I could tell that something had happened at the meeting. He entered the vehicle and he told the driver to go back to the command post. I entered the vehicle too, along with the military police officers who were escorting us. Once we were on our way, I asked the commander whether anything had happened at the meeting. He only told me: "Makso, we'll discuss this later." Probably he did not wish to discuss the meeting, because the driver was there too, as well as the military police officers. So the stretch of the road between Samac and the command post, we kept silent. He didn't talk, and I reckoned he didn't want to talk about anything. I didn't try to strike up conversation, so I kept silent too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What happened when you reached the command post in Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If we are going to have all these details as to what didn't happen and all that, we won't finish the witness. Please do lead him to the salient features of his evidence, what is relevant and what happened. We don't want all these details. They're taking too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall be finishing this section of evidence in about ten minutes, but I believe what happened at the command was very important, so I believe the witness should be able to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you arrived at the command, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we arrived there, Commander Djurdjevic asked me to come and see him in his office on the first floor. He told me that he was no longer the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. He said he had been dismissed by the Crisis Staff. It was only then I understood why he had been that agitated. I was surprised myself by these developments and by learning about this. I told him: "Well, you know very well, Commander: The Crisis Staff does not have the authority to remove you. Only whoever appointed you by order has the authority to remove you." The only thing he answered was: "Well, Makso, you know all sorts of things can happen around here."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did Commander Djurdjevic leave the command post as commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Djurdjevic left the post of commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade very soon. I think the next day he left. He reported to his Superior Command and he didn't linger; he just left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was then appointed commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While he was telling me back at the command that he had been removed, he also told me that Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, was appointed commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. After Commander Djurdjevic left, Colonel Dencic arrived as the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade at the command post in Pelagicevo. [As interpreted] He came from the command of the Eastern Bosnian Corps. He had been the commander of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. And he brought with him an order appointing Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. This order also promoted Djordjevic to the rank of lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because here on page 33, line 19, here in the transcript it says: "After Commander Djurdjevic left, Colonel Dencic arrived as the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade," which is not true. This is not what the witness said. "At the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade." Just this small correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Colonel Dencic arrived at the command post, he brought the order on appointment and promotion of Dragan Djurdjevic, Crni, as commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. He greeted Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, in a very friendly way, and the way they addressed each other was "Kume."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If you know, please tell me: Can a Corps Commander promote persons in the JNA in terms of ranks? And secondly, was that possible in the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Corps Commander could promote, but he could actually only demote. As soon as an officer had met all the requirements for promotion, yes, but the rank of lieutenant colonel, that would have been down to the General Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was then appointed chief of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srecko Radovanovic was appointed chief of the 2nd Posavina Brigade of the army of Republika Srpska. His nickname was Debeli.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was appointed commander of the military police company in the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an order. Actually, at that point no longer an order. It was a decision by the new commander, Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. The volunteer who had arrived with him - his name was Zvjezdan - he was appointed commander of the military police. To this very day, I don't know his whole name or his real name. I only know that he's called Zvjezdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you remain in your position as chief for intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remained in my position. I received no orders on my own dismissal. I remained in my position. However, I was there just for the sake of being there. No one ever called me to another meeting. I was no longer important. I would report to my Superior Command about security and intelligence. I reported to them what had happened, and they told me to just stay put, monitor what was going on, and keep on reporting, and that's exactly what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you still receive reports from Simo Zaric, as the officer for intelligence and security of the 5th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I still received those reports, but those were no longer reports in the sense in which they had been reports up to that point. We had to organise matters in a different way. I told you that my position was no longer important, so I held on to my appointment. I stayed in my position, but no one paid me any attention. I kept receiving reports, but no one called me. No one asked for my opinion. So I never offered any of my proposals to Dragan Djordjevic. He never asked for my ideas. So I just forwarded my reports to the Superior Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In which way did you communicate with Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We communicated orally. I would go to see him, and see others too. I'd never stay for very long. I did not wish to linger at the command, the way the command had become. You will understand that I reckoned that perhaps even my life was in danger. I no longer slept in the same room as before. I slept in private houses in the village of Pelagicevo. That's where I was born, so I knew people there. I'd leave my car outside one house and I'd spend the night in a different house altogether, for reasons of personal safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay with the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until July, the beginning of July, or mid-July. Major Mile Beronja was appointed commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. He was from the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And what happened to you afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Commander Beronja arrived, he bypassed all the rules and separated the security from the intelligence in the army, because at the brigade level, that was a joint thing, but at superior levels, they were separated. So he separated this at the brigade level, and he told me: "You're no longer chief of security and intelligence -- chief of security. You will from now on only be in charge of intelligence," and Captain Jez, he said, was to become chief of security. Captain Jez had arrived with him. I reported this too to my Superior Command. I was given instructions again, like I had been given instructions when Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, arrived. They told me: "Just stay put and keep a watch over what's going on."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was towards the end of August and beginning of September in 1992. I took up other duties in the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel wishes to ask questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a couple of issues to discuss with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How many questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, I have a number of topics here related to my client. Of course, I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. How many minutes do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are working today until 6.30, I believe. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. Until 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because we were informed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. That was just for -- in order to hold a Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand. Okay, Your Honour. In that case, I don't think that I will finish today, but let's see in the first couple -- let's say, half an hour or an hour how we shall go, and then I could be able to provide you with better, more precise information

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Simeunovic.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now that we're on this subject: You mentioned your permanent contact several times with the Superior Command. I believe that you are referring to the intelligence line. So what was your Superior Command along this intelligence line? Within which unit, please? Could you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In the beginning, or rather, in March, April, and the beginning of May, the Superior Command was the 17 Corps. After that, it was the Eastern Bosnian Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Specifically, the chief of security in the East Bosnian Corps; is that right? Is that a colonel? Does your superior officer have a name and surname and a rank?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, a name, surname, and a rank. It was Colonel -- now, there is a separation in terms of intelligence work and security work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Perhaps just the name.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Right this minute, I can't remember. Perhaps I'll remember later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, as an experienced soldier and intelligence man, that the principle of subordination in the military is a key principle, which means that an order has to be carried out; is that right? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, orders have to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since time is very brief, could you just give me yes or no answer? And Mr. Simeunovic, if I ask you for an explanation, then give me an explanation, please, because our time is running very short?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic. I don't mean to cut into your time unduly, but with respect to the answer that Mr. Simeunovic just gave on line 21, you had asked as to orders having to be carried out, do you agree with me? And the witness said: "Yes, orders have to be carried out." I would like to ask the witness: As a military man, does that response mean all orders, all orders which are legal, and not patently in violation of international criminal and humanitarian law? When you say: "Yes, all orders have to be carried out." Legal orders? Yes or no, if you wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When I say that orders have to be carried out, I meant orders that are in accordance with valid laws and regulations. Orders that jeopardise others, that, for example, endanger people's lives, or that would incur material damage, such orders do not have to be carried out. I remembered. The name was Colonel Jakovljevic. He was my superior along the security line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And above the East Bosnian Corps, was the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. Who was there in charge of security?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, General Tolimir was in charge of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So that is your chain of command in the army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you answered the question of honourable Judge Williams, my understanding was - and now you tell me whether I'm right - all other orders of a superior, and of a Superior Command, have to be carried out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, orders that are in accordance with valid regulations and laws have to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the order of the Presidency of the SFRY dated December 1991, on the engagement of volunteers in the armed forces of the SFRY in imminent danger of war? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You're a professional. My impression is, after your presentation now, after you answered the last questions that my colleague Mr. Pisarevic had to put to you, it was my feeling that you were personally hurt and dissatisfied with the way you were treated after Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, was appointed commander. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, I'm not a professional. I explained that at the very outset, that I was a civilian serving in the Yugoslav People's Army. As for these duties, I carried them out in a wartime unit. As for feeling hurt, I did not point out that I felt hurt, because I was not at these meetings and because I was not invited to these meetings. As a matter of fact, I can say that I can be grateful for the fact that I was not invited. I informed my Superior Command about what had happened, and I followed orders that were in accordance with regulations and laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So my conclusion is that you were satisfied with your position after Crni came as commander.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't see how you can conclude that I was satisfied. If I said that I no longer attended meetings, if I said that I could not carry out my duties --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, please, I know what you said, but the question is simple. Were you satisfied or were you unsatisfied? Please be brief and let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? What was I satisfied or dissatisfied with?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: By your very own treatment in the Brigade when Crni came as commander. It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Simeunovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please remember to pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The interpreters are having a difficult time to keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to the Trial Chamber and to the interpreters especially.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simeunovic, maybe I missed this, but what is the rank that you held in the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to the position of chief in the Tactical Group, my rank was Captain First Class.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you promoted after that when you left the army of Republika Srpska? What was the rank that you held then?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After I left -- I mean, I left bearing the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, tell me: When you were appointed chief of the security service in the 17th Tactical Group, did you have any orders? Did you have any written orders from the commander or from the command? How did your appointment take place?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The appointment was in accordance with laws and regulations of the Yugoslav People's Army. I got orders from the commander of the 17th Corps, General Sava Jankovic. That is how I was appointed chief for intelligence and security matters in the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In writing or verbally?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a written order, like all orders that are issued in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you still have that order? Do you still have it in your possession?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Simeunovic: In view of the special line of work that you had, did you complete any special courses for that particular line of work, in the period before you came to the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just say where.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I attended courses in Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There are different courses there: Beginners courses, advanced courses. Did you attend different courses there? Because we were laymen. Could you explain this to us.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Courses are organised according to the position that one holds within the establishment. I was then assistant commander for security and intelligence in a battalion, and that is where I carried out my duties, and I trained, I took a course for those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several courses. The last one was in 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you right: 1974? Isn't that a long time between 1974 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why that would be necessary. I was in the battalion all the time. It is not necessary to repeat a course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand me. Just focus, please. You said 1974. I'm asking you: Perhaps you got the figure wrong. 1974? Mr. Simeunovic, is that what you meant, 1974?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put it right. I had the last course in 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
