utterances.text: And until 1992, you did not take any other courses?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, because I completed this course at the level of assistant commander for security and intelligence in a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Before coming to the 17th Tactical Group, were you in another JNA unit?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was in the 2nd Armoured Battalion of the 395th Motorised Brigade, with its command post being in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, October 1991 was when we came to the command post in the village of Donji Zabar, the municipality of Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And before Brcko, where were you then?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was doing my work as a civilian in charge of weaponry in the 395th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me if I say that when the SFRY fell apart, and thereby the JNA fell apart as well, that former officers of the JNA went and joined their respective ethnic groups. Croats went to the Croat army, Muslims went to the Muslim army, Serbs went to the army of Republika Srpska. Is this correct what I've been saying?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this is a general truth. I think that there were people with different ethnic backgrounds who stayed in the army of Republika Srpska, and I also know that on the side of the Federation in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were some Serbs who stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, but can we concede that the majority of officers, say over 60 or 70 per cent, let's try to agree on a figure in that neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most people acted that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume that you had intelligence information about the plans of the Republic of Croatia for certain military actions in Posavina in the period before April 1992. Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have information, and we got that from Superior Commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please just give me yes or no answers.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, please don't misunderstand me. Every minute is invaluable for us. These are simple questions, and it will be quite proper in these proceedings if you'd just give yes or no answers. Believe me, there is nothing else behind this. I assume that you got this information from a network of your informers, your informers in the field who collected information. You had your own channels, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We obtained this information. As for Croatia, we got that from higher commands. We did not have our own people in Croatia with whom we could communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Another possible source would have been tapping communication lines. That's also something you do in your line of work, isn't it, and that's perfectly legitimate, I believe. I'm talking about a war situation. I'm talking about wartime. I'm not trying to confuse you. There is a war being prepared. There are two opposing sides. So you would have been perfectly entitled to tap communication lines.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to say something before I answer this question. I'm following the interpretation and I'm waiting for them to finish, and then I will say. Okay. Yes. That was one of the ways we gathered intelligence. I'm following the interpreters. I'm waiting for them to finish interpreting, and then I answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit D122/1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all very well. In the meantime, while we're waiting for this document to be shown, you will agree with me when I say that prior to April, there were a number of series armed incidents, the massacre of Serbs in Sijekovac, in Slavonia, and then in a number of towns in Posavina as a whole. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. I know about what happened in Sijekovac, a village near Bosanski Brod. Also, in Brcko there had been an attempt at sabotaging a military convoy, there were a number of such things happening, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, can you please have a look at this document and tell me if you've seen it before. While you were gathering intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps not this specific document, but I have seen documents of this kind, with this sort of content and with this heading. I have seen similar documents. Perhaps not this specific one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the signature block.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Be so kind to move a little bit the document so we can see a seal and signature. Just up, up to the -- okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question to you, Mr. Simeunovic, is: What is this position exactly, coordinator for Bosanski Brod and Derventa? I see this is the Croatian army, and we know that both Bosanski Brod and Derventa are in Bosnia. So what were your conclusions beyond the basis of intelligence gathered concerning such documents?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it says here, coordinator for Bosanski Brod and Derventa, this indicates a direct link between the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian army and forces that had been set up in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which side are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the forces set up -- such forces as the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, the army of the Croat people in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I've finished with this document. Thank you, Ms. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I want to know, Mr. Simeunovic: All this lively intelligence activity that I'm sure is quite easy to explain in times like those, full of tension. Until the 16th of April, 1992, did you have any intelligence indicating a possible attack, a joint attack by the Croat and Muslim forces on Samac and on the general area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We did have information like that, and it was precisely due to that information that Commander Nikolic ordered that part of the 4th Detachment be used to take the right-hand river bank of the River Sava and the River Bosna in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did other detachments of the 17th Tactical Group also have -- raised a state of alert in the first half of April 1992, based on the information that you had?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the detachments after the 16th of April had information that combat readiness was to be raised. Only the 4th Detachment came out on the 16th of April, because what was happening was in their area of responsibility, towards the border with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, I asked you about the period between the 1st and 16th of April, did you go home during that period? Were you relaxed? Did you have fun? What was the atmosphere like? Or quite the contrary; was there raised combat readiness among the ranks of the 17th Tactical Group, on the basis of your information? Please, tell this to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before the 16th of April, there was no raised combat readiness in any of the detachments. All detachment members were at their homes, going after their usual business. There was no raised combat readiness, and no one was told so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would like to read out a section of document P16 ter. It's a Prosecution document. This is a transcript from video footage. Stevan Nikolic and Simo Zaric were being interviewed by TV Novi Sad. First of all, let me ask you: Do you remember this programme where the two of them were interviewed in it was in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a programme like that, but that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to read a section of this tape to you, and these words are spoken by your colleague Simo Zaric. Now, tell me whether you agree with him, because, after all, you had said that you had very good cooperation and that you worked very well together as intelligence officers?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Number [Previous translation continues] ... Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "All operational information during the last couple of days indicate that in this town there is a lot of evil things in store for these people. In that sense, the 4th Detachment of the Territorial Defence was preparing for something like that to happen, and all I can say, on the basis of documents that we have, is that after war operations in this town, only three or four hours were missing for the HOS members and the Green Berets to take the city, to turn it into a city of war and to kill all the Serbs and Muslims who had formed this defence territorial component on a joint basis." Do you agree with his description of the situation? Please just give me a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To ask me now, after what you've just read, to say yes or no, I think that's simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we please have -- I believe that I distributed certain documents to Trial Chamber and also to my learned friends from the Prosecution. Our internal number is RB 19. So I'd like to discuss this document with this witness. A couple of days ago I think it was submitted. RB 19. Maybe it was your colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe I can speed up proceedings. Maybe we can discuss this document, and later on, during break, we can find where these copies are. Because I know that it was delivered. Could you place this document on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simeunovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, before we start, you say that you handed them over to the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When? Last week?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Last week, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Today is Friday, so it was last week?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: One copy for the Court officer and one for the Prosecution and one for the Registry, and three copies for the Trial Chamber as well. Your Honour, maybe during the break, if there is some problems, I can make additional copy during the break. It's only two documents that we have to discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. We don't seem to have received them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's a lot of documents. Everything is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead. You can give us copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simeunovic, have you ever seen this -- well, can you describe this for us, please? I assume these are photocopies of individual IDs issued for members of the reserve police forces of the Croatian MUP, Ministry of the Interior. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are photocopies of the front page of an official ID issued for members of the reserve police forces of the Republic of Croatia. This is noteworthy for the simple reason that these names, these members that I see here, they are citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They are not citizens of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your work, have you ever had occasion of stumbling on any of these, or have you ever seized this kind of ID off anyone in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this did happen. This is also related to the document that we've discussed today, where parties sent their own members for training with the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have your instructions whether we could tender it as an exhibit? Because I have also official translation. Or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. We have received the copies now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Oh, you have now. Can we tender it into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Prosecutor? It is just identity documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D165/1 and D165/1 ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Usher. The next document that I would like to discuss with this witness is our internal enumeration document RB 20, consisting of two pages. It's survey of paramilitary organisations in the area of responsibility of the 17th Corps. It's a two-pages document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simeunovic, can you please look at this document. We can see this is from your Superior Command, the 17th Corps. Have you ever seen this specific document before during your work?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Perhaps not this one, but I've seen another document that was identical to this one in my position of chief in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what exactly is this document, and how often would you receive this survey from your Superior Command? Once a week? Once a month? How frequently?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document represents information gathered across municipalities within the area of responsibility of the 17th Corps, information on paramilitary units set up by the SDA, HDZ, and SDS political parties. We didn't receive these surveys on a regular basis, but such surveys would come in perhaps once a month. There was no fixed deadline by which these surveys were to be delivered. Also, there would be daily additions and amendments to the surveys. We contributed our own information, our own intelligence, on which we reported to our Superior Command. They would insert the additions and then copies would be sent out to all the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you remember: These reports, were there any such reports the 17th of April, 1992, or only after the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The relationship between the JNA and the SDS was not very friendly, was it? You were not exactly allies with the SDS. What's your take on it?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think we were on the same frequency, the SDS and the JNA, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I see that in addition to the SDS, not you personally, but the army and the army's bodies, there's a remark saying that the SDS contained Chetnik units. Even this qualification shows that there wasn't much cooperation between the JNA and the SDS, was there?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said before, there certainly was no cooperation. And as for the remark, "Chetnik units," that's because certain units set up in certain municipalities called themselves Chetnik units. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Under number 4, we see Bosanski Samac municipality. The numbers, the figures speaks for themselves. There are no armed units belonging to the SDS there. Is this compatible with your personal knowledge as intelligence officer in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group and Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is consistent with the information that I had. When I spoke about this, I said that there were individual cases, but established military units belonging to the SDS, there were no such units in Samac municipality, or in a number of other municipalities, as you can see from this survey.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, can you please provide a number of explanations of the reverse side of this document. What I want to know is about the last column to the right, where it says "armed." Under number 1, for example, 30 RRB, what does that mean? What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The abbreviation "30 RRB" means they had 30 pieces of hand-held rocket launchers. RRB is an abbreviation. It stands for hand-held rocket launcher, better known as a Zolja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For example, under number 4, 10 MB, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means they had 10 mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what does this mean, number 7, Bosanski Samac, the village of Hasici, PAT 20/3? What would that mean?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: PAT means anti-aircraft gun. Number 20 is the calibre of the barrel, the calibre of the weapon. /3 means the weapon had three barrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Number 11, 40 PTR Ambrust what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means they had -- they had 40 anti-tank rockets, also referred to as Ambrust.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would like to put the following question to you: Can we agree that in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group, and in the area of responsibility where you were active as an intelligence man, there was no cooperation between the SDS and the JNA in military plans and in preparations for any kind of offensive action? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no date on this document. If it is a document after Bosnia-Herzegovina is a valid republic, the indications that these are paramilitary units are ridiculous. Actually, he has testified previously he considers paramilitary units any unit other than those tied to the JNA. In fact, after Bosnia and Herzegovina was a valid nation, had its own army, in May of 1992, he considered those armies to be paramilitary units, when in fact the JNA army, which was an army of another country on the land of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was probably the only -- was one of the paramilitary units that was probably in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. Unless you can get a date for this, this doesn't make any sense. If this is three days prior to the war beginning, then his -- these statements of paramilitary units are just not true. If it's months before, that's one thing. Is there any way we can get some sort of date for this from counsel? Because this witness didn't produce this document, and he has never seen it before, other than today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe the main part of the submission of my learned friend is for the closing arguments. This witness clearly said that he saw this kind of reports prior to 16 of April, 1992. That was my question. He confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, similar to these, not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I can clarify that immediately with him, whether it's a regular report that he was dealing with or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the other point the Prosecution is raising is that there's no date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in addition, Your Honour, since he was covering the area of Bosanski Samac, I can simply, through these questions that we already heard, establish the basis of relevance for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also the date. Because I asked him whether it's after 16th of April or prior to 16th, and he said it's prior to 16th of April, so it's in the period, obviously, let's say ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, Mr. Simeunovic: This document, and documents just like this one, did you see them in the course of your work? Did you get them from your Superior Command?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This same report, I got one from my Superior Command. Perhaps there's no date here. It can be seen that it's a photocopy, yes, but we heads of security used that, and then, on the basis of our knowledge, we could add things to this and we could send reports to the Superior Command. But this report came towards the end of April, mid-April. And before that, when I came to the command of the TG, that's when I got this, though this was the end of March 1992. That's when I got this same kind of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you look at this information, that it has to do with Bosanski Samac, the village of Domaljevac, Hasici, on page 2, you commented on that a short while ago, this information and information from item 4 of this document, or rather -- yes, it is item 4 -- does this correspond to your own intelligence information when you came to the 17th Tactical Group until the conflict broke out in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This information corresponds. When I came to the 17th Tactical Group, I got this information, that they had this information, and I also had knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Yes. The Trial Chamber is of the view that it will be admitted into evidence. What matters really is how much weight we shall put to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But we all know, Your Honours, that we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- Prosecution witnesses everything was actually corroborated with this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D166/1 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Could you move to -- I'd like to move to strike the editorial comment of the closing argument by Mr. Pantelic. On 57, lines 10 and 11, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because it doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So it will be struck off the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Simeunovic: Can we agree with the assertion that civilian authorities cannot command military units?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can. They cannot command them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Did you have any knowledge during your intelligence work about the following, namely, that the SDS was issuing military orders in Samac that were being carried out and that had to do with certain military operations? Specifically, did the SDS give orders to the 4th Detachment or the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have any such knowledge that they could have given such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: On the basis of your own intelligence data in the period that you referred to while you were in that area, did Blagoje Simic ever promote ethnic discrimination? Did your intelligence sources, or other sources, point to any such thing that Blagoje Simic publicly or in some other situations behaved that way, that is to say, along the lines of ethnic discrimination, discrimination against other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any such knowledge in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: During your work, did you have any operative information about the SDS in Samac promoting a policy of ethnic hatred, ethnic discrimination, et cetera, in the sense of political gatherings where this was talked about and so on?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we're talking about the period until the 16th of April, are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the period until the 16th of April and about the period until you held your position, that is to say, until you went to the East Bosnian Corps. So we're talking about your personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 16th of April, until what happened, happened in Bosanski Samac, we did not have any such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And after the 16th of April, did you have any knowledge to that effect, that the SDS in Samac was promoting ethnic discrimination and holding some kind of rallies? Tell us what you know about that.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any rallies. Such things were not promoted. Ethnic cleansing was not promoted at all. We did not have any knowledge about the SDS ordering ethnic cleansing or persecution. We did not have any such knowledge in the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me -- now we're moving on to a new subject. You will agree with me that the armed forces of the SFRY consisted of two components: The JNA and the TO; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is what they consisted of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were telling my colleague Mr. Pisarevic about the number of battalions and the armour used by the 17th Tactical Group, et cetera. But since we are laymen, what was the total number of soldiers under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, commander of the 17th Tactical Group while the 17th Tactical Group existed in the area? Could you give me a tentative number?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number was about 4.000 people, perhaps, who were involved in the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How many tanks did the armoured battalion have?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The armoured battalion, according to its very establishment, has 30 tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And how many did it actually have in the period while the 17th Tactical Group was there?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had 30 tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Perhaps I'm making a mistake. Correct me if I'm wrong, but it's not bad to go through this once again. You were saying to Mr. Pisarevic, in terms of the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group, tell me: On the north, it went up to the River Sava; right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To the east, it went to a village near Brcko; isn't that right? Tell me: What is the name of that village?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was between Gorica and Krepsici the village of Tinja [As interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So the south of Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell us.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the south it was the village of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one small correction on page 60. It was a river of Tinja, not village of Tinja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the witness did give this evidence already in examination-in-chief, and I don't understand why it is being repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because I didn't -- I wasn't so sure, Your Honour, that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are supposed to follow when the evidence is being given.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the west, what did you say? The municipality of Modrica to?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Gradacac to the eastern border of the municipality of Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. During your education and during your courses in intelligence, and while you held these high positions in the army, you were acquainted with the rules of service, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were also acquainted with the rules of service of the security organs of the armed forces of the SFRY; right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were also acquainted with the rules of service of the military police of the armed forces of the SFRY; right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You, as a person who -- or rather, a military person involved in the area of security, have special chains of command; right? You are not directly linked to the commander of that unit, are you?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the unit in which the security organ is, the security organ concerned is linked to the commander of the unit in terms of discipline, if we can put it that way. But in terms of security, there is a chain of command that goes to the higher security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the 17th Tactical Group, when you were there, did this chain of yours go up to which administration in the Federal Secretariat for National Defence? Was it the counter-intelligence or was it the third administration? Which one was yours, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our chain went up to the 17th Corps, not further than that. The 17th Corps, the 1st Army, the army then to the Federal Secretariat of National Defence and the General Staff. But we went up to the 17th Corps. That is our Superior Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where was General Kukanjac? What did he command?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Kukanjac was in Sarajevo. He commanded the 1st Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's the 1st or the 2nd Army, but never mind. Tell me: As the security organ, since you said that you were familiar with the rules of service of the security organs, you will agree with me that the rules of service say that you are professionally in charge of the military police organs; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We do not have the right to issue orders. Orders come from the commander. Professionally, we are engaged in professional work and we work on their improvement as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You said that the 2nd Posavina Brigade was established within the army of Republika Srpska and the Eastern Bosnian Corps. Are you aware of the order of President Karadzic dated the 13th of May, 1992, about the application of international law of war and humanitarian law? Are you aware of that order?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do we have a copy of the order to show the witness or to show --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a colloquial discussion. It's -- you know, because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are we talking about the same President Karadzic who is alleged to have violated -- who is an alleged war criminal?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It was introduced in various proceedings within this Tribunal, so it's practically a well-known document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're talking about Radovan Karadzic, the President of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who, on the 13th of May, passed that order. Are you aware of that order?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the 12th of May, when the assembly was held, and when a decision was made to establish the army of Republika Srpska, this order came too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In relation to the events that took place between the 16th and 17th of April, we will agree that perhaps a week or ten days before the 16th of April, at any rate, at the beginning of April 1992, some kind of military action took place in Modrica under the command of the commander of the 17th Tactical Group. Do you remember that? There was some skirmishes with Muslim and Croatian formations.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. This was before you said it was, I think, a little earlier. In Modrica, we received information that there was an international -- interethnic conflict in Modrica, and the JNA, which was then under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, went to Modrica. But there were no operations on the JNA's part. Not a single bullet fired. The JNA was simply there in order to show everyone who could try to provoke a conflict, that it wouldn't be possible, and the army withdrew the next day. They didn't stay in Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At any rate, Mr. Simeunovic, tensions were mounting, and the Croats were near, they were about to attack Posavina with their forces. You explained that as well already, as well as the incident at Modrica. I'll read out a section of an interview to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Number 00 -- [Previous translation continues] ... 2617, it's at page 2 of this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic told TV Novi Sad in that interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... It isn't recorded because you overlapped with the previous translation. Can you just repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll do that. So I'm speaking about document P16, the ERN number is 00892617. It's page 2. It's transcript of the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic in his interview says the following: "Over the last three or four days we've been engaged in fighting with members of the 1st Brigade of the ZNG, following their attempt to penetrate into Bosanski Samac and shatter the Serbian TO, Territorial Defence." So you did have information that the 1st Brigade of the ZNG was -- spearheaded the attack on Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have information, after the 16th of April, that an attack on Samac was in the offing, that it was being prepared. In Odzak municipality, we had several casualties on our side, and they had even more casualties than we did. There was the incident at the bridge in Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which means you had no information prior to the 16th of April that any attack on Samac had been planned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Maybe I need to correct what the witness said here. He actually said that they had one soldier dead and there were several soldiers dead on the other side. It makes a difference. It's here on page 64, lines 11 to 14, 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Simeunovic, was: Did you have intelligence or information that an attack was being prepared by the Muslim and Croat forces on Samac prior to the 16th of April, 1992, or were they friendly with the JNA and the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say anything about friendly, but we did have information that -- and we had assessments that it had been possible to put up defences for Samac along the River Sava. All the bridges had been burnt down at Orasje, and all the other bridges, so the only possibility that there was, was to transport people from Samac, and that's why we had information that the only defence they could have put up was to transfer the war operations into the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, near Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the establishment of the SDA and HDZ Crisis Staff in Samac prior to the 16th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have information that those were being established. Units of the HDZ and the SDA in Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, after listening to some of your questions, I'm wondering how helpful this evidence you are trying to elicit from this witness, how helpful it is to your client, for the defence of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. First of all -- I was just waiting for the translation to be finished. First of all, Your Honour, the count -- subcount 1 of count 1 against my client is forcible takeover. The position of the Defence is that the operation of 17th Tactical Group and JNA was in fact fully in accordance with the military doctrine, in defence of the Croatian forces, which should be operated with Croatian forces and Crisis Staff of HDZ and SDA in Samac. So that's the position of the Defence. And I want to elicit certain evidences from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic. What you just said there, frankly, I just don't understand what you've said, where you mentioned, on lines 22, 23 of page 65 that the 17th Tactical Group, JNA, was in fact fully in accordance with the military doctrine in defence of the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In defence against the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, but you actually did say "of." I heard you say that and it's recorded there in the transcript. It doesn't make any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Slip of the tongue. How can I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, good job we caught it, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Simeunovic, we are talking about the transfer of detainees from the TO, from the SUP in Samac, to Brcko. You said that some of the detainees stayed behind, that you didn't transfer all the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said some had been brought over from the SUP building in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My question to you is: People were collected at the TO building and at the SUP building in Samac. Were they all transferred to Brcko or did some of them stay in Samac? That's all I'm asking you. You were there, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there, and I said that I didn't count those people, how many exactly were being transferred, but I think they were all transferred to Brcko and that no one stayed behind in Samac. The names that Topolovac read out, they all came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the reasons for the transfer of those people to Brcko, that the reason was gathering the intelligence that those people were in possession of, concerning weapons and armament? Would you agree with me on that? Please just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's a yes or no, then I'd say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Despite your colleague Simo Zaric claiming in his book that that indeed had been the main reason, you know that he stated that in his book. Would you now change your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't change it, because I know exactly about my talks with Captain Petrovic. I know what I had been ordered by Commander Nikolic, why we were transferring those people to Samac. And as I've said before, Simo Zaric had received orders from Commander Nikolic previously to go there to look at the statements that had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just one last question before the break. Do you know the reason why some of the more prominent detainees - I mean the president of the SDA and certain people who were in high positions - why were they transferred to Batajnica, to the military airport of the JNA? Why was that? Did you receive any information as to why they were transferred to Batajnica and why they didn't stay in Bijeljina? Just tell us yes or no, please. Do you know the reason?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that at that point I had no more communication with those people. I just knew that they had been transferred to Bijeljina, but that's where my information stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's time for our break, Your Honour, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall break and continue our proceedings at 1805.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simeunovic, can you please tell me: Who initiated the transfer of prisoners from Brcko to Samac, because of the TV programme that was being planned? And hereby I mean the Muslims among them who held certain positions, Izetbegovic and the rest of them?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you bring charges against those responsible for the beating of detainees from Samac who were transferred to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean if I personally brought charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in no position to bring charges, because none of the members of the JNA were involved in the beatings of those detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: According to your information, who was involved in the beatings?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beatings were done by volunteers who had arrived from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You can look at me, not at my colleague Mr. Pisarevic, because I'm the one asking questions.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not looking at Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the sake of our communication. If those volunteers had been part of the 17th Tactical Group, would it have been possible for you to prosecute them or for the military organs to prosecute them?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would have been liable to prosecution by military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When volunteers received orders for combat operations by Commander Nikolic, in that case, would they have been part of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were taking part. Well, someone who is not a member of the 17th Tactical Group taking part in combat operations of the 17th Tactical Group, naturally, for that operation, this person would have received orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then this person would have been considered a member of the 17th Tactical Group; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps not considered a member of the 17th Tactical Group, but this person would have been under the command of the 17th Tactical Group for the duration of the combat operation. But once the operation is over, once the combat operation is completed, then this person is no longer under the command of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You said today that Simo Zaric told you, after the murder in Crkvina, that he had met Blagoje Simic and that Dr. Simic had been surprised. Tell us, please: How did he describe this to you? Was Blagoje pleasantly surprised, unpleasantly surprised, or shocked? Can you please elaborate? Because the way that it's reflected in the transcript, I think it's insufficiently described.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. As Simo Zaric said he was unpleasantly surprised. He was surprised by the incident in Crkvina and he deplored the incident at Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Why does Simo Zaric go to Belgrade to see Colonel Maksimovic at the security services? Why wasn't it you who was going there? Because you were his superior. What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was that Simo Zaric was a personal acquaintance of Colonel Jugoslav Maksimovic, who had been born in that area. I could not have gone to the General Staff myself without an order telling me explicitly to do so. I couldn't have gone from my Superior Command, as I member of the JNA. Simo Zaric went for the simple reason that he was a personal acquaintance of Jugoslav and he wanted to tell him about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you went to the 17th Corps and you told them about the incident, the crime that had occurred in Crkvina; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go. Commander Nikolic reported to the Superior Command by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The phone lines in Samac were down on the morning of the 17th of April, 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. I know that phone lines were disconnected at a later stage, but I'm not sure which period of the morning you are referring to, which time period. The phones were disconnected in the morning the next day, but as far as I knew, we did have phone connections.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The 17th of April, since when exactly did you know that phones weren't working?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the course of the day, the 17th, we didn't have any phone connections.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you specify, please, the exact hour? Was it around noon? Was it in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that when Commander Antic and Simo Zaric were there, the phone lines were still working, because they used the phone at the command to phone the detachment command. And Commander Nikolic told them to mobilise the members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At what time did that happen? Do you know, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a quarter past 6.00 or half past 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you not tell Simo Zaric at the switchboard in Samac to switch off the phones on the 17th, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between Pelagicevo and Samac in terms of kilometres?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distance is between 25 and 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At that time, how long did you take to travel from Samac to Pelagicevo by car?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a relative thing, but you would have taken between 25 and 30 minutes. Some people may have taken 20 minutes. But you could make Pelagicevo in 30 minutes, normal driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There is an armed conflict breaking out around 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning in Samac. The commander of the 4th Detachment and Simo Zaric are only arriving at your command three hours after the conflict broke out. Is that what you told Mr. Pisarevic? Do you still agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that an armed conflict had broken out. I said that when I woke up, I and other members of the command --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What time -- at what time was that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That must have been about 3.00, give or take a minute or two, but it was about 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for your subordinate, Simo Zaric, to take two hours to get from Samac to Pelagicevo? Isn't that a bit unusual? It was wartime, after all.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Nikolic, when he called the command of the 4th Detachment on the phone, he didn't tell them to be there in 30 minutes. He told them to be there the next morning. So they didn't take two hours to get there. They arrived at --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My client, Dr. Simic, claims that we have said about the phone calls, that he called Nikolic, that's simply not true. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, and I repeat what Commander Nikolic said to me, to me and to the other members of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the meeting at the heating plant. Do we agree that Colonel Djurdjevic received orders after that to take over the Brcko brigade, which is bigger, according to its establishment, than the Posavina Brigade. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After these events that took place at the heating plant in Samac, Colonel Djurdjevic was appointed commander of the 1st Posavina Brigade in Brcko. He was appointed by the command of the Eastern Bosnian Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So it is quite logical, in military service - you will agree with me - a higher command appoint its commanders to positions where they think it should be; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is why he did come as commander of the 1st Posavina Brigade. But I talked about what happened then. I don't know about the details of the conversation between Colonel Djurdjevic and the Superior Command, what they ordered him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So summarise, Mr. Simeunovic: There is not much debate, not much democracy in the military. Will we agree that he, Colonel Djurdjevic, was appointed commander of the 1st Posavina Brigade in Brcko? Yes or no? Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of the order of the superior commander, or rather, Colonel Dencic. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we agree. But while he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We don't have to go further on.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While he was in the Posavina Brigade, he did not receive orders on his dismissal or replacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after the corridor was broken through, Crni and the others were arrested and sent to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, after this corridor was broken through, that they were arrested and that they were taken to the military prison in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, from April onwards, were they in the territory of Samac all the time or did they come and go? What is your intelligence information about that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From April, when they came, especially after the conflict broke out on the 16th, they went every now and then to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you have any knowledge about the existence of some order, some written order, coming from the Superior Command, that is to say, of the East Bosnian Corps, that Colonel Djurdjevic was no longer commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such order. Perhaps it did arrive to Colonel Djurdjevic personally, but I am not aware of any such order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the information that was written on the 1st of December, 1992 and that was signed by a command consisting of 13 members, and that it had to do with some things that were taking place in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By then I had already left from the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you know about this.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it was written. I did not read it, but I know it had been written.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On page 3 of this particular information, it says: "As for the crime that was committed by Lugar in Crkvina, the Yugoslav and world press wrote about this, noting that this was being ascribed to Serbian fighters from our municipality, which meant that this weighed upon all, collectively, and people would be held accountable only after the war. In addition to that, other murders and crimes were committed. The people knew about, but remained silent, due to fear of retaliation and also because the rules of `war games.' This has to do with responsible people from our municipality, especially members of the Special Forces of Commander Crni." Did you file criminal charges against Crni and the others, and Lugar too, those who, according to some information, took part in the murders in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that the military -- or rather, Yugoslav People's Army --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army did not file any criminal charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were criminal charges filed within the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because they were not members of the army of Republika Srpska either, or of the Yugoslav People's Army, when the crime was committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And do you know that they were held accountable before the military court in Banja Luka, that is to say, the army of Republika Srpska, because of the killing of a scout? Are you aware of that? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that after the corridor was closed, they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just say yes or no. So say: Yes, I am aware of it --

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that they were in military prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, before you continue, I just wanted to put the exhibit number of the document from which you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: 127, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Hmm?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: P127, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Isn't it logical, Mr. Simeunovic, that you're saying that you know that the army of Republika Srpska, in its court, conducted proceedings against volunteers from Serbia because of the killing of a scout and proceedings were not carried out because of the crime that was committed in Crkvina? How come there is this duality? Sometimes they are under the authority of army of Republika Srpska and sometimes they are not. Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that I was aware of proceedings being instituted. I just said that I know that they were taken to the military prison in Banja Luka. But whether proceedings were instituted against them is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simeunovic. As a security officer and as a man who is a professional, you are aware of the provisions of the Geneva Conventions; is that right? You were exchanged -- you were involved in exchanges later in the army, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are familiar with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I read out to you from the decision regarding General Blaskic, paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask Mr. Pantelic to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And which document is that? Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is a judgement of General Blaskic. It's not a document. It's in judgement. It's a part of the judgement of General Blaskic. I want to put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, this is Article 86, Your Honour, of Additional Protocol, nothing more. It's well-know fact. And he's familiar with Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read this out to you slowly, or rather, you will receive interpretation of this. So this is paragraph 325 from General Blaskic's judgement. It is Article 86, paragraph 2 of Additional Protocol I. [In English] "The fact that a breach of the Conventions or of this Protocol was committed by a subordinate does not absolve his superiors from penal or disciplinary responsibility, as the case may be. If they knew or had information which should have enabled them to conclude in the circumstances at the time that he was committing or was going to commit such a breach and if they did not take all feasible measures within their power to prevent or repress the breach." [Interpretation] Do you agree with this? This is Additional Protocol I; right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 329 of the Blaskic judgement - this is Article -- this relates to Article 87, paragraph 1 of the Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions, and this article should be viewed in the spirit of the previous one. It reads as follows ... "The high contracting parties and the parties to the conflict shall require military commanders with respect to members of the armed forces under their command, and other persons under their control, to prevent and, where necessary, to suppress and to report to competent authorities breaches of the conventions and of this protocol." [Interpretation] You agree with this, don't you? I'm asking you whether you agree with this, what I've just read out.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 319 of the Blaskic judgement, the hostage case is quoted, and it reads as follows: [In English], "Commanding general of occupied territory is charged with the duty of maintaining peace and order, punishing crime, and protecting lives and property within the area of his command. His responsibility is coextensive with his area of command. He is charged with notice of occurrences taking place within that territory. He may require adequate reports of all occurrences that come within the scope of his power, and if such reports are incomplete or otherwise inadequate, he is obliged to require supplementary reports to apprise him of all the pertinent facts. If he fails to require and obtain complete information, the dereliction of duty rests upon him and he is in no position to plead his own dereliction as a defence. Absence from headquarters cannot and does not relieve one from responsibility for acts committed in accordance with the policy he instituted or in which he is acquainted." [Interpretation] Do you agree with this, Mr. Simeunovic?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska and the military prosecutor's office, on the 1st of October, 1992, adopted guidelines for setting criteria for criminal prosecution. On page 14 of these guidelines of the military prosecutor's office, it says, page 14 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because I'm not aware of this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, that's -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, it's not an exhibit. It's just a document which is within the, you know, knowledge of each professional who is dealing with the International Criminal Tribunal. I mean, it's in the library, so it can be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I must say that I personally am not familiar with this document. It might be useful for us to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: -- have the possibility of seeing it before -- for us to be informed with respect to you questioning the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's just his personal knowledge or maybe I will put to him certain portions of this document and simply to say whether he's agree or not. It's not the matter of the document by itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but what we are saying is that we haven't got sight of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's a document from Krstic case, and it is -- it can be found in the library. I can just say that at this moment I just want to -- not to discuss this particular document, but rather, the events or principles of the penal and criminal proceedings within the army of VRS and his personal position towards that. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, we will stop eliciting evidence at this stage, because the Trial Chamber has some rulings to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm fully aware about the instructions, but can I just briefly inform you about the problems that I am suffering? I would like to have just five minutes to finish with this witness, with my cross-examination, because I have commitments with regard to the organisation of videolink and certain problems on the field and stuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Well, as long as you don't refer to the document which seems to be unknown. So you'll wind up your cross-examination, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Simeunovic, you are aware of the fact that the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska cautioned all commanders in the field that they should collect appropriate information about war crimes and that they should prosecute persons who committed such acts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander was duty-bound to collect information on crimes that were committed by members of the military who were under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. You also know about certain efforts that were made and certain instructions that were given by the Main Staff to prevent looting and other crimes in the areas of responsibility of Republika Srpska; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that pertained to the members of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me: In your work, while you worked for the army of Republika Srpska and within the 17th Tactical Group, did you ever file criminal charges against any perpetrators on account of looting, murder, or any other criminal act?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for murder. Not a single criminal report. Criminal reports were filed for looting. What later happened, how the military courts treated the report, I don't know, but there were no murders committed by members of the army of Republika Srpska in our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you file any criminal reports for war crimes or violations of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No such thing happened while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group and the 2nd Posavina Brigade, there were no war crimes, according to you.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those members who were under the command of the army of Republika Srpska, or the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade and the TG at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I've finished my cross-examination. Thank you very much, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Simeunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, did you have questions?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd have about one, one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will continue the proceedings on Monday with this witness. Can the witness be led out of the courtroom, please. Mr. Simeunovic, you'll continue your evidence on Monday. The proceedings will be in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The videolink proceedings will start on Tuesday, because they have to use Monday to put up the equipment. The Trial Chamber has a ruling on the Rule 92 bis statements regarding the defence of Mr. Blagoje Simic. The Trial Chamber has examined the witness statements submitted under the provisions of Rule 92 bis on behalf of the accused Dr. Blagoje Simic. In most cases, the statements have complied with the provisions of the Rule. However, where the acts and conducts of the accused, as alleged in the indictment, have been included, the Trial Chamber has considered whether, in fact, such acts and conduct, as still contentious as the rest of the evidence so far on record has shed light on what elements of the crimes charged. The Trial Chamber has to decide, when considering liability. The Trial Chamber has also considered the opportunities the Prosecution has had for cross-examination for those statements where the evidence is mostly cumulative. The Trial Chamber has observed that viva voce witnesses so far heard, and those to be heard, judging by their summaries, mostly overlap, so that it is only necessary, in the view of the Trial Chamber, to allow cross-examination where the evidence is mainly peculiar to each individual accused, besides being contentious generally. The Trial Chamber has, at the same time, taken care that each accused person's right to call evidence or witnesses in his own defence is not undermined. After the said considerations, the Trial Chamber has decided that, of the statements submitted on behalf of Dr. Blagoje Simic so far, only one witness will be called to give evidence viva voce regarding matters touching on the conduct and activities of the accused, as alleged in the indictment. This is Witness Cedomir Simic, whose statement is D163/1, and the viva voce evidence will be restricted to matters stated in paragraph 20, since that part of the statement is not admitted into evidence. The rest of the statement is admitted into evidence. The Prosecution will be allowed to cross-examine this witness, and the time limit allowed for the cross-examination will be one and a half hours, whereas the time allowed to elicit the evidence concerning the events described in paragraph 20 will be one hour. The statements made by -- the statement made by Witness Amir Lukic, that is D159/1, will be admitted into evidence, except that paragraph 2 will be struck out, as pointed out by the Prosecution and as decided by the Trial Chamber. Only the first and the last sentence of that paragraph will remain on record. If I may add, the Trial Chamber is able to distinguish fact from opinion. This witness will not be cross-examined. The statement by witness Mitar Ibralic, that is D160/1, will be admitted into evidence without cross-examination. The statement by Nerzija Ordic, D161/1, will be entered into evidence without cross-examination. The statement of Perica Krstanovic, D162/1, will be admitted into evidence without cross-examination. However, part of paragraph 7 will be struck out, that is, the words in parenthesis, beginning with " for example" and ending with "Serbian children." That part will be struck off the statement. The rest of the paragraph remains. In the same statement, paragraph 14 is struck out in its entirety. This witness, that is, Perica Krstanovic, will not be cross-examined. Father Jovo Lakic is a character witness, and his statement, 164/1, will be admitted into evidence without cross-examination. Mijo Babic is also a character witness, and the statement D158/1 -- paragraphs 11, 12, 13, and the last sentence of paragraph 14 are struck out of the statement. The rest of the statement is admitted into evidence and he will not be cross-examined. The remaining statements for the other two accused, Mr. Simo Zaric and Mr. Miroslav Tadic, will be decided upon in the course of next week or soon after the videolink witnesses. The Trial Chamber would like to discuss the witnesses for the videolink, which is starting on Tuesday. The Trial Chamber has information that Mirko Pavic, it's no longer possible for him to speak or that he has suffered a stroke since. Or what is the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we, during our last stay, in fact, Mr. Pisarevic's stay in Belgrade -- sorry -- in Bosanski Samac, he took a statement from Mr. Mirko Pavic and a certification of this statement is already made. So when Mr. Pisarevic came back here in The Hague - it was on Monday - he gave this statement for translation. We are not aware of, at this point, what his medical condition of Mr. Mirko Pavic. We can check that and inform the Trial Chamber. What I can tell the Trial Chamber is that we do have 92 bis statements, 35, according to 92 bis Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The representative of the Registry was present when Mr. Pavic signed this statement. He can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's not the problem. What the Trial Chamber was concerned with is whether or not he will be able to appear for cross-examination, if the Trial Chamber rules that he has to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point, we don't have a hundred per cent certain information. Mr. Pisarevic will be in Bosanski Samac as for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And he will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Be able to find out the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- whether he is able to give his tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And I want to confirm with the Prosecution that this statement by Mirko Pavic was given to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there was a more recent 92 bis certification. I don't think it's been translated yet. We're still waiting for a number of them, including some which were certified, I believe, on our last day in Belgrade, deposition. I don't believe it's one of them that we received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber had instructed the legal officer to discuss this particular one with the Prosecution and ask them to have it translated for their own use in case they need to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it. Maybe it was done with Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, most likely. Then you'll be able to find out in due course over the weekend. That leaves us with Savo Popovic and Mustafa Pistolevic and Milutin Grujicic as the rest of the witnesses. Most of the evidence that has been admitted through the 92 bis statements for Dr. Blagoje Simic will make it necessary for you, Mr. Pantelic, to reduce the area of examination for the witnesses that you have lined up, because you will see that most of the evidence is already covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may ask for -- maybe I didn't understand well. You mean for the next witnesses in this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. For the one on videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Oh, you mean Savo Popovic. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will be -- I can tell you, I already provided just for the record a brief summary of facts to the Prosecution of the facts on which the -- Mr. Savo Popovic will testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also the focus of my examination will be events in Odzak, military administration, and certain events within Crisis Staff in Samac. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm saying is if you look at the statements that have been admitted under Rule 92 bis, you will find that a lot of the evidence is overlapping, so you should be able to make it as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: People, they have same story, you know, that I cannot control. I mean, try -- I understand the position, but sometimes it was very hard to limit it, these people, from the evidence. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is there any other matter to be raised by the parties? I see none. We shall rise and continue our proceedings on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of March 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
